analysis.one_liner: Caps total federal emergency bailout payments to any single company at $150 billion.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Banking Committee with no hearing, no vote, and not a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set a hard ceiling of $150 billion on the total amount of federal emergency bailout money — under the 2008 Troubled Asset Relief Program or any similar program — that any one company and its affiliates could receive. It was aimed at limiting the giant rescues of individual financial firms during the financial crisis, under which single companies had drawn support running into the hundreds of billions. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who under the 2008 bailout program were exposed to the full cost of rescuing individual financial giants; the bill would have capped how much public money any single firm and its affiliates could absorb.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers exposed to giant bailout costs

how_it_helps.text: It barred the government from paying any single person or company — including its affiliates — more than $150 billion in total under TARP or any other federal emergency economic assistance program.
It overrode ('notwithstanding any other provision of law') any earlier legal authority that allowed unlimited emergency payments, hard-wiring a ceiling into statute.

analysis.who_pays: Any systemically important firm in distress that could no longer be fully supported past $150 billion, and potentially the broader financial markets if a disorderly failure followed; in normal times, virtually no one, since the cap only bound the largest recipients.

drawbacks.text: The cap applied 'notwithstanding any other provision of law' and set a hard dollar ceiling with no exception for a firm whose collapse mid-crisis could cascade through the financial system, so a rigid statutory limit could have forced the government to stop supporting a failing giant mid-rescue.

A firm could have stayed just under the $150 billion cap and still received enormous support, so the limit addresses only the very largest recipients rather than reining in the bailout program as a whole.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was real but blunt: a hard $150 billion ceiling would have limited the Treasury's open-ended exposure to any one failing company, and the record shows at least one recipient had already drawn more than that. The cost is that a statutory cap with no flexibility, applied "notwithstanding any other provision of law" [S3], could have stopped the government mid-rescue of a systemically important firm and let a panic spread — a tradeoff the bill never addressed, and one the committee evidently judged not worth taking up.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 24, 2009, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs — the only committee action ever taken.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.

The bill would have capped, at $150 billion in the aggregate, all payments to any person or company including affiliates under the Troubled Asset Relief Program or any other federal emergency economic assistance program.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large firms receiving federal rescue payments benefited from the status quo: no limit was ever placed on how much support any one of them could receive, and taxpayers continued to carry the full exposure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big bailout recipients and their creditors

for.name: Sen. James Inhofe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap aggregate federal emergency assistance to any single recipient at $150 billion and delivered introductory remarks; it was referred to the Banking Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Sen. Christopher Dodd, D-CT)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no one cosponsored, so the partisan shape of support and opposition cannot be measured; the bill died from inaction rather than a recorded fight.

industries.industry: Large bailed-out financial firms (e.g., giant insurance and bank holding companies receiving TARP support)
industries.note: The bill would have capped total federal emergency assistance to any company and its affiliates at $150 billion, limiting the open-ended rescue support the biggest firms could draw. Ordinary taxpayers bore the risk of those payments, so the firms' interest here ran against the public's.
